speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) whether Singapore has plans to stockpile uranium to secure energy sources ahead of other countries shifting towards nuclear energy; and (b) what preparations are being made to prepare a core of local talent to enter this industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: So, what we are doing is steadily building capabilities to better understand and assess global developments on advanced nuclear energy technologies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask how many scientists are currently at the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Initiative and how many scholarships are awarded each year to help build the pipeline of nuclear scientists and expertise?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Beyond technical capabilities, is the Government building up the necessary regulatory policy frameworks that will be needed to oversee potential nuclear energy programmes for both nuclear fission and nuclear fusion?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, is there any timeline in which the Government is going to take a position on this?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think he has asked about three of them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We did our last nuclear energy pre-feasibility study in 2012.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And since that pre-feasibility study, the National University of Singapore has set up the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Initiative (SNRSI) in 2014, and SNRSI focuses on research and capability development in nuclear safety, science and engineering.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government has also set up the Nuclear Safety Research and Education Programme under the Research Innovation and Enterprise 2025 plan to prepare Singapore to understand the implications of the evolution of nuclear energy technologies and regional nuclear energy developments for Singapore, and also to enhance our operational preparedness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To his first point in terms of the numbers, Sir, the Government supports efforts to train scientists and experts in local and overseas universities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As for his last point on looking at nuclear fission and nuclear fusion, maybe I can address nuclear fusion first.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is a lot of excitement in the fusion space but to date, on the sustainable basis, the net energy input needed to create that nuclear fusion reaction far exceeds the output of the energy that we can harness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the closest system that many of the countries all over the world have developed still is premised on the tokamak technology.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is a promising new area, which is done in Devon, Massachusetts in the United States by Commonwealth Fusion Systems.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They are developing this as a sort of a co-development with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Plasma Science and Fusion Center, and it is called SPARC.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is a smaller-scale tokamak reactor, uses high temperatures super magnets to create the high temperature that is needed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To date, it is still a developmental project.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The actual project has not come to fruition yet.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are watching that space very closely and in the process, we have also sent members of the local Singapore team to go there and study how that technology is going to evolve.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, for nuclear fusion, to answer the question, I think it is still quite nascent and we are probably at least a decade away.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For nuclear fusion, there are small modular reactors, there are also Generation 4 thermal reactors which potentially could suit our needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, again, we have teams studying those technologies very closely, very intently.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But today, there is not a commercialised small modular nuclear reactor or a Generation 4 thermal reactor for us to be able to learn from.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In our broad approach, as I have said before, nothing is off the table.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We continue to keep our options open to all kinds of low carbon energy, including of course nuclear energy, both fission and fusion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Just that last question – when is the Government going to take a position on whether to use nuclear energy in our energy mix in the future?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does the Minister agree that it is important to provide some certainty or more certainty to both aspiring scientists and our people with regard to the use of nuclear energy?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, we recognise the fact that radiological safety, the understanding of the operational capabilities, the engineering science behind it, continues to be something that is important and relevant to us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, we have not stopped training our local pipeline of talent, sending them overseas, attaching them to institutions all over, collaborating with them to learn and to adapt that expertise and invite the knowledge, so that at some point in time when we have finally made the decision, we will then bring them back here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think this is a very clear enough roadmap given the nascency of the commercialisation of some of these newer generations type of small modular reactors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For fusion, as I have said earlier on, today, the net energy input put in to develop that fusion reaction is far more than what we are able to extract from it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, net-net, it does not make economic sense in any way for us to go into it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But having said that, we are still nonetheless studying that, monitoring that space very closely.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think this is as far as we can tell you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will not be able to commit to a particular timeline, but that does not mean that we stop looking at it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have said today, our pipeline in the medium to long term is 100 researchers at least.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And for our own energy security, we also do not rest on one or two technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have improved the diversification of our sources of procurement for natural gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think I have spent a lot of hours in this House explaining, expounding why we need to diversify our gas sources.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, those are the different alternatives that we are now exploring, on top of also keeping our eyes on nuclear energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that gives the Member the reassurance.
